description: Decisions made without enough information, and what the field does with its errors. This pack carries the most risk and the most reward. Order matters: ask the judgment questions first, because they establish that you understand the job is hard, which is what makes the failure questions feel like curiosity rather than prosecution.

questions.text: Tell me about a call you had to make without enough information.
questions.lands_because: Universal condition of professional work, and it lets the guest look competent while being honest about uncertainty. A reliable story generator.
followups: What would you have needed to know to be sure?
Did you ever find out whether you were right?

questions.text: What is a tradeoff you make constantly that would alarm an outsider?
questions.lands_because: Every field rations something - time, attention, risk, care - and practitioners normalize it. Naming it out loud is genuinely revealing and often the clip that travels.
followups: Is that the right tradeoff? What would it take to change it?
questions.avoid_if: You have not yet established that you understand the constraints they work under. Without that, the answer becomes a confession they will regret.

questions.text: What is more dangerous in your work - moving too fast or moving too slow? Has your answer changed over your career?
questions.lands_because: Forces a real position rather than a both-sides answer, and the career-arc half invites reflection instead of defensiveness.

questions.text: What does your gut tell you that you have learned to override? And what have you learned to trust?
questions.lands_because: Intuition calibration is the interior experience of getting good at something, and the two-part structure keeps it from becoming a platitude about trusting yourself.

questions.text: Who do you call when you are stuck?
questions.lands_because: Small, easy, and it maps the informal expertise network that every profession runs on and no org chart shows.
followups: What do they have that you do not?

questions.text: What is a mistake you made early that you now watch for in other people?
questions.lands_because: The safest possible entry into failure. It is framed as mentorship, it is safely in the past, and it almost always yields a real story rather than a sanitized one.
followups: What did it cost at the time?

questions.text: How does your field handle error? Is there a formal process, or does it just get absorbed?
questions.lands_because: Structural rather than personal, so it is easy to answer honestly - and the answers vary enormously. Aviation and medicine have formal review; most fields absorb error silently, and that contrast is itself the story.
followups: What happens to the person who made the error?

questions.text: Tell me about a near-miss - something that almost went badly and did not.
questions.lands_because: Near-misses carry the dramatic weight of failure without the shame of it, so guests tell them freely. Often the best story in the episode.
followups: Did anything change afterward, or did everyone just move on?

questions.text: When something goes wrong in your work, who finds out and who does not?
questions.lands_because: Goes at disclosure norms rather than at the guest personally. Reveals the accountability structure of an entire industry in one answer.

questions.text: What is the cost of being wrong in your job, and who actually pays it?
questions.lands_because: The second clause is the sharp one. In some fields the practitioner pays; in others a patient, a client, a homeowner, or a taxpayer does. It surfaces the moral weight of the work directly.
followups: Does that asymmetry change how carefully you work?
questions.avoid_if: The guest is currently facing litigation, an investigation, or a public incident.

questions.text: Is there one you are still carrying?
questions.lands_because: Short, quiet, and unguarded. It works only as a follow-on, after the guest has already told you a failure story and found that you handled it well.
questions.avoid_if: Never open with this, and never ask it of a guest who has stayed guarded. If they deflect, let it go on the first deflection - pushing here costs you the rest of the interview.
